title: Getting Out of the Way of Something That Moves: Guessing Where It Is Going, Looking Along the Plan for the Moment They Meet, and Choosing Between Waiting and Going Round

questions.question: How does a track get a velocity?
options: From the difference between successive sightings over the time, smoothed
From a single sighting and its time stamp
questions.explanation: Two places and the time between them. A share of 0.7 of each new difference smooths it: 0.499 m/s for a true 0.5 after six sightings.

questions.question: An arm that did not look was how far from the obstacle at the closest?
questions.explanation: The sphere rose into the path as the tool reached it. The arm that stopped kept 0.031 m, and the one that went round 0.135 m.

questions.question: Waiting and planning round took:
questions.explanation: Stopping and going on when clear cost 0.65 s over the free move. Planning a way round and taking it cost far more.

questions.question: A meeting with an obstacle 1 m away coming at 0.5 m/s was predicted how far away?
options: 2.00 s, the distance over the speed
questions.explanation: The gap that has to close is the metre less the radii and the margin, at half a metre a second.

questions.question: Why does the monitor go on looking after a new plan?
options: The new plan may be longer than the old
The track's velocity needs more sightings
The obstacle may run into the new plan too: a plan is a promise about a world that moves
The planner may not have finished
questions.explanation: The new path was made for where the obstacle was. It keeps moving, and may move into the new path as well.

questions.question: When is waiting better than going round?
options: When the thing is about to go away; a long detour is for nothing
When the arm is far from its goal
When a new plan would be shorter
questions.explanation: Waiting cost 0.65 s and going round 2.70 s. For something passing through, the detour is the worse choice; the trouble is knowing which it is.
